extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers seeking an overview of Hwang Woo-suk and the associated scientific-ethics controversy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing Hwang Woo-suk's career, alleged achievements, subsequent investigations into ethical and scientific misconduct, legal outcomes, and later activities. It provides narrative accounts, quotations, and references about research practice, investigations, and public/political responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary informed consent for egg donations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether egg donations were truly voluntary and not coerced — the Nature article raised the question 'whether the students might have been pressured to give eggs and thus whether such a donation would have been "voluntary" as Hwang claimed in his scientific paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents allegations of payments to donors (e.g., US$1,400 each), use of graduate students' eggs, and later panel findings that Hwang distributed egg-donation consent forms and personally escorted a researcher to a hospital for extraction. These facts are presented as breaches of ethical norms surrounding informed consent and donor procurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific verifiability and data transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Research claims must be supported by scientifically verifiable data rather than media sessions or photo ops — the article notes Hwang 'failed to provide scientifically verifiable data, giving only media sessions and photo ops.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry documents concrete failures (missing raw data, duplicated photos, lack of original records) and explains that verifiable laboratory records, unique images, and reproducible experimental data are required to substantiate extraordinary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of data fabrication and image/data integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and images must not be fabricated or duplicated; the page reports that several photos 'of purportedly different cells were in fact photos of the same cell' and that nine of eleven cell lines were fabricated according to DNA evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of fabrication cited includes identical DNA profiles across cell lines and duplicated images. Such indicators were central to the university panel's finding of intentional fabrication and to Science's unconditional retraction of the papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship responsibility and publication ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are expected to have declared full confidence in submitted work; journals and co-authors have rules about retraction and name removal — 'No single author, having declared at the time of submission his full and complete confidence in the contents of the paper, can retract his name unilaterally, after publication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts Gerald Schatten asking to be removed and Science's refusal, and notes that Science unconditionally retracted the 2004 and 2005 papers after confirmation of fabrication. It implies authorship accountability and journal procedures for handling suspected misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with bioethics laws and international ethical declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Research involving human materials must comply with bioethics laws and guidelines such as the Declaration of Helsinki — the article notes Hwang claimed unfamiliarity with the Declaration, which 'clearly enumerates his actions as a breach of ethical conduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links breaches (egg procurement, payments, coercion) to violations of ethical norms and national bioethics statutes, and records that Hwang was charged with bioethics law violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use and accounting of research funds (no embezzlement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research funds must not be misappropriated; prosecutors charged Hwang with embezzlement and misusing tens of millions of won of state and private research funds for personal purposes and illicit payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed allegations include diversion of funds through accounts held by relatives/subordinates, cash withdrawals, buying gifts, and illegal payments to ova donors; the page lists investigators' tracking of specific sums and items (cars, political funds), showing financial transparency and lawful use as evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent verification and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary claims should be independently reproduced or subjected to outside analysis — scientists called on Hwang to 'submit his paper to an outside group for independent analysis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records calls from prominent researchers that independent replication or external tests could settle disputes; independent genetic testing later confirmed that Snuppy was indeed a clone, illustrating the role of external verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate characterization of biological origin (cloning vs parthenogenesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must correctly identify and report the biological process that produced cell lines; later chromosomal analyses showed indicators of parthenogenesis rather than somatic cell nuclear transfer cloning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains that chromosome evidence distinguished parthenogenetic origin and notes the panel's remark that the team did not conscientiously probe the parthenogenesis possibility using available tests. Proper diagnostic testing and correct interpretation are required for valid claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional investigatory procedures and evidentiary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities and panels investigating misconduct may seal laboratories, collect testimonies, analyze lab records, and compare claimed protocols with documentation to determine fabrication or misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Seoul National University panel sealed Hwang's lab, collected testimonies, reviewed egg counts and records (finding discrepancies between claimed and recorded egg use), and issued a final report confirming fabrication—demonstrating procedural steps and evidentiary checks used in such probes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/employment rules during investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional rules can restrict actions like resignation while under investigation — 'a university regulation that dictates that an employee under investigation may not resign from a post' to avoid evasion of retribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seoul National University cited this regulation when refusing Hwang's resignation request, and later suspended and dismissed him after the investigation, showing how administrative policies govern employment outcomes during misconduct probes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic ethics in investigative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative journalism should avoid coercive or ethically dubious methods; the MBC program PD Su-cheop was criticized for coercive tactics in interviews and faced sponsorship withdrawal and scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes media backlash, sponsor withdrawal, and debates over whether critical reporting was 'unpatriotic' or ethically problematic, illustrating the tension between exposing wrongdoing and adhering to journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about political ties and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers and institutions must disclose conflicts of interest and political connections that may influence funding or public promotion — the article documents Hwang's active seeking of political ties and government awards/funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hwang's relationships with government advisors, receipt of honors (e.g., 'Supreme Scientist'), and large funding tied to his claimed results are presented as context for potential conflicts and as factors that affected public/political responses when accusations arose.
